PHIL 100.title: Introduction to Philosophy
PHIL 100.description: Basic problems and methods of Philosophy. Topics such as the existence of God, the nature and scope of human knowledge, the relationship between mind and body, personal identity, free will, issues and problems in moral philosophy.

PHIL 101.title: Introduction to Philosophy
PHIL 101.description: Basic problems and methods of philosophy. Topics such as the nature and scope of human knowledge, the existence of God, and the relationship between mind and body.

PHIL 102.title: Introduction to Philosophy II
PHIL 102.description: Basic problems and methods of philosophy. Topics such as morality, personal identity, free will and determinism, and the meaning of life.

PHIL 104.title: Happiness
PHIL 104.description: What makes for deep, lasting happiness, joy, and wellbeing? Contemporary and classical works of philosophy and important debates in related fields such as psychology, economics, political theory, and sociology.

PHIL 120.title: Introduction to Critical Thinking
PHIL 120.description: Tools for dealing with both everyday and more technical arguments and concepts. Analysis and resolution of confusions, ambiguities, and fallacies. This course is restricted to students with fewer than 90 credits.

PHIL 125.title: Introduction to Scientific Reasoning
PHIL 125.description: Historical and logical analysis of various types of scientific hypotheses and the data that support or undermine them. This course is restricted to students with fewer than 90 credits.

PHIL 211.title: Greek Philosophy I: Socrates and Plato
PHIL 211.description: The Pre-Socratics; Socrates; Sophists; Plato. Recommended as preparation for PHIL 310.

PHIL 212.title: Greek Philosophy II: Aristotle and After
PHIL 212.description: Aristotle; selections from Hellenistic and Late Antique Philosophy. Recommended as preparation for PHIL 310.

PHIL 220.title: Symbolic Logic
PHIL 220.description: Sentential and predicate logic. Translation from natural language; truth tables and interpretations; systems of natural deduction up to relational predicate logic with identity; alternative proof methods. Some sections may use computer-based materials and tests.

PHIL 222.title: Enriched Symbolic Logic
PHIL 222.description: Naïve set theory, relations and functions, recursion and induction; Propositional and predicate logic; Symbolizations, semantics, and formal proof theory; Metatheory for propositional logic. Recommended for students interested in pursuing upper-level courses in logic or formal philosophy.

PHIL 230.title: Introduction to Ethics
PHIL 230.description: Theories of obligation and value; moral reasoning; normative ethics, descriptive ethics and meta-ethics. Readings in classic and contemporary texts.

PHIL 235.title: Contemporary Moral Issues
PHIL 235.description: Moral issues such as life and death decisions, paternalism, markets, animal welfare, technology, and global justice.

PHIL 240.title: Introduction to Epistemology
PHIL 240.description: Topics in epistemology such as skepticism, truth, justification, a priori and a posteriori knowledge. Readings from classic and contemporary texts.

PHIL 250.title: Minds and Machines
PHIL 250.description: Philosophical and theoretical issues that pertain to how mental phenomena fit into the material world. Examine questions such as whether a sophisticated enough computer should be deemed a conscious intelligent being. Focus on philosophical literature on consciousness, intelligence, animal minds, and the mind-body relation.

PHIL 260.title: Science and Society in the Contemporary World
PHIL 260.description: An introduction to the historical development, conceptual foundations, and cultural significance of contemporary science. Themes will vary from year to year.

PHIL 310.title: The Philosophy of Plato
PHIL 310.description: A study of Plato's dialogues and his influence on subsequent philosophy. PHIL/CLST 211 or AMNE 235 and PHIL/CLST 212 or AMNE 236 are recommended.

PHIL 311.title: The Philosophy of Aristotle
PHIL 311.description: A study of Aristotle's writings and his influence on subsequent philosophy. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL 310.

PHIL 313.title: Medieval Philosophy
PHIL 313.description: Survey of Western European thought from Augustine to the 14th century. Possible topics and authors include: Augustine; Abelard; the influence of Islam; the rediscovery of Aristotle; Aquinas; Scotus; Ockham.

PHIL 314.title: Philosophy in the 17th Century
PHIL 314.description: Survey of 17th-century philosophy from Bacon to Leibniz, including the writings of Hobbes, Descartes, and Spinoza. The influence of science and religion on philosophy.

PHIL 315.title: Philosophy in the 18th Century
PHIL 315.description: Survey of 18th-century philosophy from Locke to Kant, including the writings of Berkeley, Rousseau, and Hume. The influence of science and religion on philosophy.

PHIL 316.title: Philosophy After 1800
PHIL 316.description: Survey of 19th and 20th century philosophy. May include Hegel, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Mill, Meinong, Brentano, the British Idealists, Russell, and Moore. Social and political currents in 19th century philosophical thought.

PHIL 320.title: Logic: Metatheory and Computability
PHIL 320.description: Continuation of PHIL 220. A system of deduction for predicate logic is selected for further study. Completeness of this system and other metatheoretic results are proved. Other topics include computability, recursive function theory, incompleteness and decidability. Recommended pre-requisite: one of PHIL 220, PHIL 222. PHIL 222 is recommended.

PHIL 321.title: Induction, Decision and Game Theory
PHIL 321.description: Formal methods relevant to probabilistic and inductive reasoning. Decision theory, game theory, axiomatic probability theory and its interpretations, belief dynamics, simulation and modelling. Recommended pre-requisite: one of PHIL125, PHIL 220, PHIL 222 or instructor permission.

PHIL 322.title: Modal Logic
PHIL 322.description: Logic of the modal operators It is necessary that and It is possible that. Possible-world semantics and a method of derivation for this logic. Recommended pre-requisite: one of PHIL 220, PHIL 222. PHIL 222 is recommended.

PHIL 323.title: Non-Classical Logics
PHIL 323.description: One or more of conditional logic, deontic logic, epistemic logic, many-valued logic, systems of belief dynamics. Recommended pre-requisite: one of PHIL 220, PHIL 222. PHIL 222 is recommended.

PHIL 324.title: Philosophy of Logic
PHIL 324.description: Fundamental concepts and methods of logic; the logistic method, syntax and semantics; the conditional; entailment; consequence; modal logic; problems concerning extensionality and intentionality. Frege's distinction between sense and reference; Russell's theory of definite descriptions; Tarski's definition of truth. Recommended pre-requisite: one of PHIL 220, PHIL 222. PHIL 222 is recommended.

PHIL 326.title: Philosophy of Language I
PHIL 326.description: Philosophical discussion of language, meaning, and communication.

children.raw: plus 6 additional credits of PHIL/LING at the 200-level or above

PHIL 326.prerequisiteText: At least one of LING 201/PHIL 220/PHIL 222, plus 6 additional credits of PHIL/LING at the 200-level or above

PHIL 330.title: Social and Political Philosophy
PHIL 330.description: Theories of political and legal obligation and authority, legal reasoning, society and the state. Readings in classic and contemporary texts.

PHIL 331.title: Business and Professional Ethics
PHIL 331.description: Moral problems in contemporary business and professional practice, general moral theory, the law, and policy formation. Corporate social and environmental responsibility, employee rights, preferential hiring and affirmative action programs, conflicts of interest, advertising, whistle blowing and self-regulation.

PHIL 332.title: Environmental Ethics
PHIL 332.description: Moral problems arising in the context of human relationships to nature and to non-human living things, considered in terms of both general moral theory and policy formation. Topics include moral standing, animal rights, obligations to future generations, pollution, hazardous materials, the depletion of natural resources and the treatment of non-human living things.

PHIL 333.title: Bio-Medical Ethics
PHIL 333.description: Moral problems arising in the health sciences, especially in medicine but also in biology, psychology, and social work. Topics include abortion, death and euthanasia, genetic engineering, behaviour modification, compulsory treatment, experimentation with human beings and animals, and the relationship between professionals and their patients, subjects or clients. No philosophical background is required.

PHIL 334.title: Sex, Gender and Philosophy
PHIL 334.description: Relationship between sex, gender, and philosophy. Topics may include ethics, epistemology, science, social relations, law, and personhood.

PHIL 335.title: Power and Oppression
PHIL 335.description: Philosophical approaches to historical problems of inequality and social harm, with readings drawn from historical and contemporary sources. Topics to be studied may include slavery, colonialism, labour, and the position of women in society.

PHIL 336.title: Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, and Ethics
PHIL 336.description: Survey of the main ethical questions and challenges from mass data collection and analysis, automated decision making, and artificial intelligence. Some prior study of philosophical ethics and data analysis is helpful but not required. Recommended for both Major in Philosophy students and other students interested in this topic.

PHIL 337.title: Ethics for the Sciences
PHIL 337.description: Philosophical exploration of ethical issues in the non-medical sciences, including topics such as intellectual integrity, responsible conduct of research, protection of human subjects, ethics of animal experimentation, and the social responsibilities of scientists.

PHIL 338.title: Philosophy of Law
PHIL 338.description: Concepts of law, constitution and sovereignty; law and morality; natural law theories and legal positivism; obligation, responsibility, and punishment.

prerequisite.raw: Restricted to second- or higher-year standing

PHIL 338.prerequisiteText: Restricted to second- or higher-year standing

PHIL 339.title: Philosophy of Art
PHIL 339.description: Topics include art and perception, art and reality, imagination, expression, censorship, and the role of art in human life.

PHIL 340.title: Introduction to Metaphysics
PHIL 340.description: Topics in metaphysics such as the nature of physical reality, personal identity, the mind/body problem, free will, causation and action theory. Readings from classic and contemporary texts.

PHIL 347.title: Philosophy of Religion
PHIL 347.description: A critical and analytical examination of arguments for and arguments against the existence of God, and other related topics.

PHIL 348.title: Introduction to Continental Philosophy
PHIL 348.description: Major themes and figures in the Continental philosophy tradition; possible topics include 19th century precursors, 20th century philosophers, and comparisons between analytic and continental philosophy.

PHIL 351.title: Philosophical Perspectives on Cognitive Systems Research
PHIL 351.description: Philosophical exploration of questions and theories arising from research into the mind, as conducted in psychology, linguistics, and computer science.
PHIL 351.prerequisiteText: 3 credits selected from any of PHIL 211, 212, 220, 222, 230, 235, 240, 250, 260, or COGS 200

PHIL 360.title: Introduction to History and Philosophy of Science
PHIL 360.description: An examination of historical, conceptual and methodological conditions of scientific knowledge through detailed consideration of important episodes in the history of science.

PHIL 362.title: History and Philosophy of Economics from Aristotle to Adam Smith
PHIL 362.description: The development of economic thought from Aristotle to Adam Smith, focusing primarily on the conceptual foundations of economics, particularly the problems of value, distribution, and economic growth. A maximum of 6 credits will be granted for PHIL_V 362 or ECON _V 318.

PHIL 363.title: History and Philosophy of Economics from Ricardo to Keynes
PHIL 363.description: The development of economic thought from David Ricardo up to the present, including such figures as Mill, Jevons, and Keynes, focusing primarily on the conceptual foundations of economics, particularly the problems of value, distribution and growth. A maximum of 6 credits will be granted for PHIL_V 363 or ECON_V 319.

PHIL 364.title: Darwin, Evolution, and Modern History
PHIL 364.description: Darwin and the science of evolution in nineteenth and early twentieth century.

PHIL 369.title: Philosophy of Science
PHIL 369.description: Issues common to all sciences. Philosophical questions including the character of scientific laws, theories and revolutions, the nature of scientific confirmation, causality, explanation and prediction, and the use of logic and probability. Difficulties in the interpretation of atomic physics and questions about relationships between biology and psychology. No philosophical background is assumed.

PHIL 371.title: Foundations of Chinese Thought
PHIL 371.description: Early (pre 221 BCE) Chinese thought (Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, Legalism), its contemporary implications, and the role of philosophy and religion in human flourishing./

PHIL 375.title: Philosophy and Literature
PHIL 375.description: Philosophical issues in works of literature or arising from theories of literary interpretation. Topics include issues relating to relativism, the nature of morality, free will, personal identity, the nature of the emotions.

PHIL 378.title: Philosophical Wisdom of Early India
PHIL 378.description: Epistemological and ontological thought from the Vedic Period to the period of the rise of philosophical schools or systems. Philosophy in the Mahabharata, Gita; early Buddhist and Jain views on knowledge and reality; views on language.

PHIL 385.title: Existentialism
PHIL 385.description: Meaning, identity and alienation as explored in the works for example of Kierkegaard, Dostoyevsky, Tolstoy, Sartre, and Camus.

PHIL 388.title: Classical South Asian Philosophy
PHIL 388.description: Debates on issues of epistemology, language and ontology among the philosophical traditions of classical South Asia. PHIL 378/ASIA 378 is recommended.

PHIL 400.title: Morals, Politics and the Individual
PHIL 400.description: Introduction to major themes in moral and political philosophy. Primarily for fourth-year and graduate students who have had no previous course in Philosophy.

PHIL 401.title: Knowledge, Explanation, and the Nature of Things
PHIL 401.description: Introduction to major themes in epistemology and metaphysics. Primarily for fourth-year and graduate students who have had no previous course in Philosophy.

PHIL 410.title: Topics in Ancient Philosophy
PHIL 410.description: Advanced study of the Presocratics, or of a philosopher such as Plato, or of a school such as the Sceptics or Stoics. Topics vary from year to year. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL 311.

PHIL 412.title: Topics in Medieval Philosophy
PHIL 412.description: Advanced study of a medieval philosopher such as Aquinas, or school. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL 313.

PHIL 414.title: Topics in the History of Modern Philosophy
PHIL 414.description: Intensive study of a major philosopher or school such as Descartes, Hume, Empiricism, Rationalism, or the British utilitarians. Recommended pre-requisites: one of PHIL 314, PHIL 315, PHIL 316.

PHIL 415.title: The Philosophy of Immanuel Kant
PHIL 415.description: Study of Kant's critical philosophy. Recommended pre-requisite: one of PHIL 314, PHIL 315, PHIL 340

PHIL 416.title: Topics in 19th-Century Philosophy
PHIL 416.description: Study of a major 19th-century philosopher such as Hegel, Mill or Nietzsche, or school, such as German Idealism. Recommended pre-requisites: one of PHIL 314, PHIL 315, PHIL 316, PHIL 340.

PHIL 418.title: Topics in Twentieth-Century Philosophy
PHIL 418.description: Intensive study of a major philosopher such as Wittgenstein, Russell, or Heidegger, or school, such as pragmatism or logical empiricism. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL 340.

PHIL 419.title: Philosophy of History
PHIL 419.description: Concepts of history and historical explanation, historical progress, purpose, necessity, law and causation. Hegel, Marx, Vico, Spengler, Pareto, Collingwood, Croce, and Toynbee, as well as contemporary figures. Students will be expected to have an adequate knowledge of ancient or modern history.

PHIL 420.title: Topics in Symbolic Logic
PHIL 420.description: Formal semantics, proof theory, incompleteness and decidability, axiomatic set theory, independence results. Consult the Department as to which topics are offered in a given year.

PHIL 426.title: Topics in Philosophy of Language
PHIL 426.description: Advanced topics in the philosophy of language. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL 326 and 6 credits of PHIL/LING at the 200-level or above.

PHIL 427.title: Philosophy of Mathematics
PHIL 427.description: Logicism, formalism and constructivism, implications of metatheorems such as those of Gödel and Church, mathematical truth, mathematics and mental construction, mathematics and the physical world.

prerequisite.raw: Philosophy or mathematics courses totaling 9 credits at the 200-level or above

PHIL 427.prerequisiteText: Philosophy or mathematics courses totaling 9 credits at the 200-level or above

PHIL 431.title: Topics in Social and Political Philosophy
PHIL 431.description: Central concepts and problems in political life and thought including obligation, citizenship, representation, justice; equality; civil rights and liberty; disobedience.

prerequisite.raw: 9 credits of PHIL_V/POLI_V at the 200-level or above

PHIL 431.prerequisiteText: 9 credits of PHIL_V/POLI_V at the 200-level or above

PHIL 432.title: Topics in Ethical Theory
PHIL 432.description: Classic or contemporary works in ethical theory.

children.raw: 9 credits of PHIL_V at the 200-level or above

PHIL 432.prerequisiteText: PHIL_V 230. 9 credits of PHIL_V at the 200-level or above

PHIL 440.title: Topics in Epistemology
PHIL 440.description: Analysis of the concept of knowledge; problems of justifying ordinary and basic empirical beliefs. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL_V 240.

PHIL 441.title: Philosophy of Perception
PHIL 441.description: The contribution of the senses to knowledge of the external world; the nature of perception and its contribution to empirical knowledge. Recommended pre-requisites: Either (a) PHIL 240 or (b) COGS 200. If COGS 200, accompanied by 3 credits in PHIL at the 200-level or above.

PHIL 448.title: Topics in Continental Philosophy
PHIL 448.description: A study of European philosophers from amongst Husserl, Heidegger, Habermas, Foucault, Derrida, Lacan, Levinas, and others.

PHIL 450.title: Topics in Metaphysics
PHIL 450.description: Topics including ontology, universals and particulars, substance, determinism and indeterminism, identity over time, and theories of truth.

prerequisite.raw: 9 credits in PHIL at the 200-level or above

PHIL 450.prerequisiteText: 9 credits in PHIL at the 200-level or above

PHIL 451.title: Philosophy of Mind
PHIL 451.description: The nature of the mental and physical; the relation between minds and bodies; the character of psychological explanation. Recommended pre-requisites: Either (a) PHIL 240 or (b) COGS 200. If COGS 200, accompanied by 3 credits of PHIL at the 200-level or above.

PHIL 452.title: Philosophy of Action
PHIL 452.description: Explanation of human actions; the conditions of responsibility; freedom of the will; the domains of rational and moral appraisal; the category of action and the individuation of actions. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL 340.

PHIL 455.title: Topics in the Philosophy of Cognitive Science
PHIL 455.description: Philosophical topics in the cognitive sciences, such as empiricism vs. nativism, consciousness, mental representation, cognitive architecture, language & thought, and situated cognition.

children.raw: any 6 credits of Philosophy at the 200-level or above

PHIL 455.prerequisiteText: One of PHIL 441, PHIL 451. Or any 6 credits of Philosophy at the 200-level or above (except PHIL 220, PHIL 222, PHIL 320)

PHIL 461.title: Philosophy of Social Science
PHIL 461.description: Topics in the philosophy of science of special concern to the social sciences: the problem of objectivity, the use of models and evidence, causation and causal reasoning, formal methods, the status of social kinds and norms, scientific explanation, laws.

prerequisite.raw: 9 credits at the 200-level or above from philosophy, anthropology, geography, economics, history, political science, psychology or sociology

PHIL 461.prerequisiteText: 9 credits at the 200-level or above from philosophy, anthropology, geography, economics, history, political science, psychology or sociology

PHIL 462.title: Space and Time
PHIL 462.description: Such topics as: Are space and time continuous? Is motion always relative to another body? Does time flow? Is time irreversible? Recommended pre-requisites: PHIL 340 or 12 credits of mathematics or science.

PHIL 464.title: Philosophy of Biology
PHIL 464.description: Methodological, historical, philosophical and social science questions about biology.

prerequisite.raw: Fourth-year standing in any degree program or 9 credits of philosophy

PHIL 464.prerequisiteText: Fourth-year standing in any degree program or 9 credits of philosophy

PHIL 469.title: Topics in Philosophy of Science
PHIL 469.description: Topics such as probability and induction; foundations of measurement; theory construction. Recommended pre-requisite: PHIL_V 369.

PHIL 470.title: Comparative Conceptions of the Self
PHIL 470.description: Ways in which the 'self' has been portrayed in eastern and western religious traditions. Thinkers to be considered include Aristotle, Mencius, Freud, Xunzi (Hsn-tzu), Nietzche, and Zhuangzi (Chuang-tzu).

PHIL 491.title: Seminar for Majors in Philosophy
PHIL 491.description: Selected problems in philosophy, with attention to methods of research. Check with the department for specific topics. Primarily for fourth-year Philosophy Major students, but also open to Philosophy Honours.

PHIL 528.title: Philosophical Issues in the Foundations of Mathematics

PHIL 534.title: Issues in Business and Professional Ethics

PHIL 561.title: Topics in Science and Technology Studies
PHIL 561.description: Advanced seminar on a theme or topic of interest to both STS and Philosophy.
